parts.latex:
Jenny's class completes two tests.

For the first test, the mean was 63.2 and the standard deviation was 5.5.

For the second test, the mean was 70 and the standard deviation was 7.5.

Jenny scored 72 on the first test. Calculate the mark that she needed to obtain in the second test to ensure that her performance relative to the class was maintained.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By using $z$-scores and the standard normal distribution table, find the probability that a randomly chosen competitor achieves a final height between 5.99 and 7.19 metres.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Harrison is one of the competitors. The height of his jump is greater than approximately 29.8% of all competitors. Find the height of his jump.

solutions.latex:
Cars : motorbikes $= 8:3$ and motorbikes : vans $= 5:2$, so (matching motorbikes) cars : motorbikes : vans $= 40 : 15 : 6$.

40 parts $= 160$ cars, so 1 part $= 4$ cars.

$160 + (15 \times 4) + (6 \times 4) = 244$ vehicles

$3\text{ cm} = 1.5\text{ m}$

$3.5\text{ cm} = 1.75\text{ m}$

$1.75 \times 1.5 = 2.625\text{ m}^2$

Accept $1.7 \times 1.45 = 2.465\text{ m}^2$
It does not separate the source and sink completely.

First test: $z = \dfrac{72 - 63.2}{5.5} = 1.6$

Second test: $1.6 = \dfrac{x - 70}{7.5}$

$1.6 \times 7.5 = x - 70$

$x = (1.6 \times 7.5) + 70$

$\therefore x = 82$

Greater than $29.8\%$.

$1 - 0.298 = 0.702 \approx 0.7019$, so $z = 0.53$.

Since he is greater than only $29.8\%$, $z$ must be negative (use symmetry, same probability), so $z = -0.53$.

$-0.53 = \dfrac{x - 5.36}{3}$

$x = (3 \times -0.53) + 5.36$

$\therefore x = 3.77$ metres
